Main.sentence: Havana ( /həˈvænə/ ; ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ : La Habana [la aˈβana] ⓘ )  is the capital and largest city of ___E:Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba)___ .
The heart of ___E:La Habana Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Habana_Province)___ , Havana is the country's main port and commercial center.

It is the most populous city, the largest by area, and the ___E:second largest metropolitan area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_the_West_Indies)___ in the ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ region.

The population in 2021 was 2,142,939 inhabitants,   and its area is 728.26 km 2 (281.18 sq mi)  for the capital city side and 8,475.57 km 2 for the metropolitan zone.  Its official population was 1,749,964 inhabitants in 2024.
Havana was founded by the ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire)___ in the 16th century.

It served as a springboard for the ___E:Spanish conquest of the Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas)___ , becoming a stopping point for Spanish ___E:galleons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galleon)___ returning to Spain.

King ___E:Philip III of Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_Spain)___ granted Havana the title of capital in 1607.  Walls and forts were built to protect the city.  The city is the seat of the ___E:Cuban government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Cuba)___ and various ministries, and headquarters of businesses and over 100 diplomatic offices.

The governor is ___E:Reinaldo García Zapata U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinaldo_Garc%C3%ADa_Zapata)___ of the ___E:Communist Party of Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Cuba)___ (PCC).
In 2009, the city/province had the third-highest income in the country.

Contemporary Havana can essentially be described as three cities in one: ___E:Old Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Havana)___ , ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ and the newer suburban districts.

The city extends mostly westward and southward from the ___E:bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Harbor)___ , which is entered through a narrow inlet and which divides into three main harbors: ___E:Marimelena, Guanabacoa and Antares U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Harbour#Facilities)___ .

The ___E:Almendares River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almendares_River)___ traverses the city from south to north, entering the ___E:Straits of Florida U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Florida)___ a few miles west of the bay.
The city attracts over a million tourists annually;  (1,176,627 international tourists in 2010,  a 20% increase from 2005).

Old Havana was declared a ___E:UNESCO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO)___ ___E:World Heritage Site U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site)___ in 1982.  The city is also noted for its ___E:history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Havana)___ , culture, architecture and monuments.
As typical of Cuba, Havana experiences a ___E:tropical climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate)___ .
In 1514, Diego Velázquez founded the city San Cristóbal de la Habana, which means " ___E:Saint Christopher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Christopher)___ of the Habana".

It has been theorized that the name is derived from ___E:Habaguanex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habaguanex)___ , who was the chief of a local ___E:Taíno U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%ADno_language)___ -speaking Native American people group about whom nothing else is known.

When Habana was adapted into English, the ⟨b⟩ was switched to a ⟨v⟩ because of a linguistic phenomenon known as ___E:betacism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betacism)___ , which is an assimilation of the ___E:voiced bilabial plosive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_bilabial_plosive)___ and ___E:voiced labiodental fricative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_labiodental_fricative)___ sounds that occurs in most modern Spanish dialects.

Usage of the word Havana in literature understandably peaked during the ___E:Spanish–American War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War)___ , but it also represents a type of cigar, a color, and a type of rabbit as well as the city.  Havana is the prevailing name for the city found in English-language dictionaries.

___E:Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Vel%C3%A1zquez_de_Cu%C3%A9llar)___ founded Havana in 1514, on the southern coast of the island, near the present town of Surgidero de ___E:Batabanó U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataban%C3%B3,_Cuba)___ on the banks of the ___E:Mayabeque River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayabeque_River)___ close to ___E:Playa Mayabeque U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playa_Mayabeque)___ .
All attempts to found a city on Cuba's south coast failed, however; an early map of Cuba drawn in 1514 places the town at the mouth of the river.

Between 1514 and 1519 the Spanish established two settlements on the north coast, one of them in La Chorrera , around the site of the ___E:Torreón de la Chorrera U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre%C3%B3n_de_la_Chorrera)___ , what eventually became the neighborhoods of Vedado and Miramar, next to the mouth of the ___E:Almendares River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almendares_River)___ .

The town that became Havana originated adjacent to what was then called Puerto de Carenas (literally, " ___E:Careening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Careening)___ Port"), in 1519. The quality of this natural bay, which now hosts Havana's harbor, warranted this change of location.
___E:Pánfilo de Narváez U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A1nfilo_de_Narv%C3%A1ez)___ gave Havana – the sixth town founded by the Spanish on Cuba – its name: San Cristóbal de la Habana .
The name combines San Cristóbal , ___E:patron saint U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint)___ of Havana.
Shortly after the founding of Cuba's first cities, the island served as little more than a base for the Conquista of other lands.

Havana began as a trading port, and suffered regular attacks by ___E:buccaneers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buccaneer)___ , pirates, and ___E:French corsairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_corsairs)___ .

The first attack and resultant burning of the city was by the French corsair ___E:Jacques de Sores U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_de_Sores)___ in 1555. Such attacks convinced the Spanish Crown to fund the construction of the first fortresses in the main cities – not only to counteract the pirates and corsairs, but also to exert more control over commerce with the West Indies, and to limit the extensive contrabando ( ___E:black market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_market)___ ) that had arisen due to the trade restrictions imposed by the Casa de Contratación of ___E:Seville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville)___ (the crown-controlled trading house that held a monopoly on New World trade).
Ships from all over the New World carried products first to Havana, to be taken by the fleet to Spain.
The thousands of ships gathered in the city's bay also fueled Havana's agriculture and manufacture, since they had to be supplied with food, water, and other products needed to traverse the ocean.

On 20 December 1592, ___E:King Philip II of Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Philip_II_of_Spain)___ granted Havana the title of City. Later on, the city would be officially designated as "Key to the New World and Rampart of the West Indies" by the ___E:Spanish Crown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Crown)___ .
In the meantime, efforts to build or improve the defensive infrastructures of the city continued.
Havana expanded greatly in the 17th century.

New buildings were constructed from the most abundant materials of the island, mainly wood, combining various ___E:Iberian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ architectural styles, as well as borrowing profusely from ___E:Canarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_islands)___ characteristics.
During this period the city also built civic monuments and religious constructions.

The convent of St Augustin, El Morro Castle, the chapel of the Humilladero, the fountain of Dorotea de la Luna in La Chorrera, the church of the Holy Angel, the ___E:hospital de San Lázaro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_de_San_Lazaro,_Havana)___ , the monastery of Santa Teresa and the convent of San Felipe Neri were completed in this era.
In 1649 a fatal epidemic, brought from ___E:Cartagena U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia)___ in Colombia, [citation needed] affected a third of the population of Havana.
In 1674, the works for the City Walls were started, as part of the fortification efforts.
They would be completed by 1740.

By the middle of the 18th century, Havana had more than seventy thousand inhabitants, and was the third-largest city in the Americas, ranking behind Lima and Mexico City but ahead of Boston and New York City.

During the 18th century Havana was the most important of the Spanish ports because it had facilities where ships could be refitted and, by 1740, it had become Spain's largest and most active shipyard and only ___E:drydock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drydock)___ in the New World.
The city was captured by the British during the ___E:Seven Years' War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years%27_War)___ .

The ___E:episode U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Havana_(1762))___ began on 6 June 1762, when at dawn, a British fleet, comprising more than 50 ships and a combined force of over 11,000 men of the ___E:Royal Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy)___ and Army, sailed into Cuban waters and made an amphibious landing east of Havana.

The British immediately opened up trade with their ___E:North American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American)___ and ___E:Caribbean colonies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_West_Indies)___ , causing a rapid transformation of Cuban society.

Less than a year after Havana was seized, the ___E:Peace of Paris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1763))___ was signed by the three warring powers thus ending the Seven Years' War. The treaty gave Britain ___E:Florida U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Florida)___ in exchange for the return of the city of Havana on to Spain.

After regaining the city, the Spanish transformed Havana into the most heavily fortified city in the Americas like ___E:Cartagena, Colombia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia)___ a city that under the leadership of ___E:Blas de Lezo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blas_de_Lezo)___ defeated a British invasion of 30,000 sailors.

Construction began on what was to become the Fortress of ___E:San Carlos de la Cabaña U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Caba%C3%B1a)___ , the third biggest Spanish fortification in the New World after ___E:Castillo San Cristóbal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_San_Crist%C3%B3bal_(San_Juan))___ (the biggest) and ___E:Castillo San Felipe del Morro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_San_Felipe_del_Morro)___ both in San Juan, Puerto Rico. On 15 January 1796, the remains of ___E:Christopher Columbus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus)___ were transported to the island from ___E:Santo Domingo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Domingo)___ .
They rested there until 1898, when they were transferred to ___E:Seville's Cathedral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral)___ , after Spain's loss of Cuba.

As trade between Caribbean and North American states increased in the early 19th century, Havana became a flourishing and fashionable city. Havana's theaters featured the most distinguished actors of the age, and prosperity among the burgeoning middle-class led to expensive new classical mansions being erected.
During this period Havana became known as the Paris of the ___E:Antilles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antilles)___ . [citation needed]

In 1837, the first railroad was constructed, a 51 km (32 mi) stretch between Havana and ___E:Bejucal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bejucal)___ , which was used for transporting sugar from the valley of ___E:Güines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCines)___ to the harbor.
With this, Cuba became the fifth country in the world to have a railroad, and the first Spanish-speaking country.

Throughout the century, Havana was enriched by the construction of additional cultural facilities, such as the ___E:Tacón Theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Theatre_of_Havana)___ , one of the most luxurious in the world.

The fact that slavery was legal in Cuba until 1886 led to Southern American interest, including a plan by the ___E:Knights of the Golden Circle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_the_Golden_Circle)___ to create a ___E:'Golden Circle' U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Circle_(proposed_country))___ with a 1200 mile-radius centered on Havana.

After the ___E:Confederate States of America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America)___ were defeated in the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ in 1865, many former slaveholders continued to run plantations by moving to Havana. [citation needed]
In 1863, the city walls were knocked down so that the ___E:metropolis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis)___ could be enlarged.
At the end of the 19th century, Havana witnessed the final moments of Spanish presence in the Americas.

The sinking of the ___E:U.S. battleship Maine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Maine_(ACR-1))___ in Havana's harbor in 1898 was the immediate cause of the ___E:Spanish–American War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War)___ .

Cuba's first presidential period under ___E:Tomás Estrada Palma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom%C3%A1s_Estrada_Palma)___ from 1902 to 1906 was considered to uphold the highest standards of administrative integrity in the history of the Republic of Cuba.

While Cuba had the highest ratio of hospital beds to population in the Caribbean, around 80% of these beds were located in the city of Havana, there was only one rural hospital and it was equipped with only 10 beds. In July 1940, during ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , the ___E:Havana Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Conference_(1940))___ was held and 21 American nations, including the host country Cuba, agreed to govern their own territories that were occupied by the ___E:Axis powers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers)___ .
In 1958, Cuba was a relatively well-advanced country by Caribbean standards, and in some cases by world standards.
Cuba was affected by perhaps the largest labor union privileges in the Americas, including bans on dismissals and mechanization.
They were obtained in large measure "at the cost of the unemployed and the peasants", leading to disparities.
Between 1933 and 1958, Cuba extended economic regulations enormously, causing economic problems.

Unemployment became a problem as graduates entering the workforce could not find jobs. The middle class, which was comparable to that of the United States, became increasingly dissatisfied with unemployment and political persecution.
The labor unions supported Batista until the very end. Batista stayed in power until he was forced into exile in December 1958.

After the ___E:revolution of 1959 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Revolution)___ , the new government under ___E:Fidel Castro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro)___ began to improve social services, public housing, and official buildings.

Nevertheless, after Castro's abrupt expropriation of all private property and industry (May 1959 onwards) under a strong communist model backed by the Soviet Union followed by the U.S. ___E:embargo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_embargo_against_Cuba)___ , shortages that affected Cuba in general hit Havana especially hard. By 1966–68, the Cuban government had ___E:nationalized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalized)___ all privately owned business entities in Cuba, down to "certain kinds of small retail forms of commerce" as per law No. 1076.

An economic downturn occurred after the ___E:collapse of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ in 1991. Soviet subsidies ended, representing billions of dollars that the Soviet Union had given the ___E:Cuban government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba_%E2%80%93_Soviet_Union_relations)___ .
Many believed the revolutionary government would soon collapse, as happened to the Soviet ___E:satellite states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_state)___ of Eastern Europe.

Tourism in Cuba has brought foreign investors to remodel the nationalized, former Manzana de Gomez building, and turn it into the ___E:Gran Hotel Manzana Kempinski La Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Hotel_Manzana_Kempinski_La_Habana)___ , a new ___E:5-star U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_rating)___ hotel attempting to develop a new hospitality industry.
In Old Havana, a number of streets and squares have been rehabilitated in an effort to rebuild for tourists.
But Old Havana is a large city, and the restoration efforts concentrate in all on less than 10% of its area.
On the night of 27 January 2019, an unusually violent and destructive ___E:tornado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado)___ ripped through Havana.

The tornado killed eight people and injured over 190. It was assigned an official rating of EF4 on the ___E:Enhanced Fujita scale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale)___ by the Cuban Meteorology Institute, making this the first F4 or EF4 tornado in Cuba since 1940.
The Havana City Council first started in 1550.
In 1557, the Council voted to ban all freed black men from owning taverns, inns, selling tabaco, or wine.
Under the ___E:Captaincy General of Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Cuba)___ , the Havana City Council existed.

After the ___E:Cuban War of Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_War_of_Independence)___ , Cuba created a new constitution in 1901.  The Havana City Council was re-inaugrated on July 2, 1901.  Alfredo Zayas was briefly appointed mayor, followed by the installment of ___E:Miguel Gener y Rincón U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Gener)___ , the acting Secretary of Justice of Cuba,  after winning the ___E:1900 Cuban local elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Cuban_local_elections)___ .

In 1902, pending an investigation by ___E:Emilio Núñez U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez)___ , Gener was removed as mayor of Havana by ___E:Leonard Wood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Wood)___ , after a vote of twenty-three out of twenty-five members of the City Council requested him to do so.
Under the Communist administration, the administrative makeup of the city was re-structured.
The governor is ___E:Reinaldo García Zapata U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinaldo_Garc%C3%ADa_Zapata)___ ,  he was elected on 18 January 2020.

The city is administered by a city-provincial council, with a governor as chief administrative officer,  thus Havana functions as both a city and a province of Cuba. The city has little autonomy and is dependent upon the national government, particularly, for much of its budgetary and overall political direction.
Voters elect delegates to Municipal Assemblies in competitive elections every five years, and the Municipal Assemblies are responsible for each of the city's boroughs.
These assemblies elect the borough presidents and vice presidents, which are equivalents to mayors and vice mayors in the other provinces.

There is only one political party, the ___E:Communist Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Cuba)___ , but since there must be a minimum of two candidates, members of the Communist Party often run against each other.
Candidates are not required to be members of the party.
They are nominated directly by citizens in open meetings within each election district.

Municipal Assembly delegates within the boroughs in turn elect members of the Provincial Council (until 2019 the Provincial Assembly), which in Havana serves roughly as the City Council; its president appoints the Governor and Vice Governor, who serve as the Mayor and Vice Mayor of Havana and can be either elected by the council or appointed by the president with council confirmation.
There are direct elections for the city's deputies to the National Assembly based on slates, and a portion of the candidates is nominated at the local level.

The People's Councils (Consejos Populares) consist of local city delegates who elect a full-time representative to preside over the body. These councils are directly responsible for the city's neighbourhoods and wards.
In addition, there is involvement of "mass organizations" and representatives of local government agencies, industries and services.
The 105 People's Councils in Havana cover an average of 20,000 residents. [citation needed]

Havana city borders are contiguous with the ___E:Mayabeque Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayabeque_Province)___ on the south and east and to ___E:Artemisa Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemisa_Province)___ on the west, since former ___E:La Habana Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Habana_Province)___ (rural) was abolished in 2010.

Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the ___E:Straits of Florida U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Florida)___ , south of the ___E:Florida Keys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys)___ , where the ___E:Gulf of Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico)___ joins the Atlantic Ocean.
The city extends mostly westward and southward from the bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and which divides into three main harbors: Marimelena, Guanabacoa, and Atarés.
The ___E:Almendares River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almendares_River)___ traverses the city from south to north, entering the Straits of Florida a few miles west of the bay. [citation needed]
There are low hills on which the city lies rise gently from the waters of the straits.

A noteworthy elevation is the 200-foot-high (60-meter) limestone ridge that slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of ___E:La Cabaña U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Caba%C3%B1a)___ and ___E:El Morro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_de_los_Tres_Reyes_del_Morro)___ , the sites of Spanish fortifications overlooking the eastern bay. Another notable rise is the hill to the west that is occupied by the ___E:University of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Havana)___ and the ___E:Castillo del Príncipe (Havana) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_del_Pr%C3%ADncipe_(Havana))___ . [citation needed]

Havana has a ___E:tropical climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate)___ that is tempered by the island's position in the belt of the ___E:trade winds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_wind)___ and by the warm offshore currents. [clarification needed] Under the ___E:Köppen climate classification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification)___ , Havana has a ___E:tropical savanna climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_savanna_climate)___ ( Aw ) that closely borders on a ___E:tropical rainforest climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_rainforest_climate)___ ( Af ) and a ___E:tropical monsoon climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_monsoon_climate)___ ( Am ).
Average temperatures range from 22 °C (72 °F) in January and February to 28 °C (82 °F) in August.
The temperature seldom drops below 10 °C (50 °F).
The lowest temperature was 1 °C (34 °F) in Santiago de Las Vegas, Boyeros.
The lowest recorded temperature in Cuba was 0 °C (32 °F) in Bainoa, ___E:Mayabeque Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayabeque_Province)___ (before 2011 the eastern part of Havana province).
Rainfall is heaviest in June and October and lightest from December through April, averaging 1,200 mm (47 in) annually.
Hurricanes occasionally strike the island, but they ordinarily hit the south coast, and damage in Havana has been less than elsewhere in the country.
The most recent tropical cyclone to come near Havana at hurricane strength was ___E:Ian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian)___ in 2022.

Tornadoes can be somewhat rare in Cuba. Nonetheless, on the evening of 28 January 2019, a very rare strong ___E:EF4 tornado struck the eastern side of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Havana_tornado)___ .

The tornado caused extensive damage, destroying at least 90 homes, killing four people and injuring 195.     By 4 February the death toll had increased to six, with 11 people still in critical condition.

The city is divided into 15 municipalities  – or boroughs , which are further subdivided into 105 consejos populares (wards)
By the end of 2012 official Census, 19.1% of the population of Cuba lived in Havana.
According to the census of 2012, the population was 2,106,146.  The city has an average ___E:life expectancy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy)___ of 76.81 years at birth.
Havana agglomeration grew rapidly during the first half of the 20th century reaching 1 million inhabitants in the 1943 census.
The con-urbanization expanded over the Havana municipality borders into neighbor municipalities of Marianao, Regla and Guanabacoa.

Starting from the 1980s, the city's population is growing slowly as a result of balanced development policies, low birth rate, its relatively high rate of emigration abroad, and controlled domestic migration.

Because of the city and country's low birth rate and high life expectancy,   its age structure is similar to a developed country, with Havana having an even higher proportion of elderly than the country as a whole.
According to the 2012 national census of Havana's population (the Cuban census and similar studies use the term "skin color" instead of "race").

As with the other Caribbean nations, there are few ___E:mestizos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizos)___ in Havana (and Cuba as a whole), in contrast to many other countries, because the indigenous ___E:Taíno U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta%C3%ADno)___ population was virtually wiped out by Eurasian diseases in the earliest period of the Spanish conquest.

The Cuban government controls the movement of people into Havana on the grounds that the Havana metropolitan area (home to nearly 20% of the country's population) is overstretched in terms of land use, water, electricity, transportation, and other elements of the urban infrastructure.

There is a population of internal migrants to Havana nicknamed "palestinos" (Palestinians)  who mostly hail from the eastern region of ___E:Oriente U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriente_Province)___ .

The city's significant minority of Chinese, mostly of ___E:Cantonese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese_people)___ origin, were brought in the mid-19th century by Spanish settlers via the ___E:Philippines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines)___ with work contracts and after completing 8-year contracts many Chinese immigrants settled permanently in Havana.

Before the revolution the Chinese population counted to over 200,000,  today, Chinese ancestors could count up to 100,000.  [failed verification] Chinese born/ native Chinese (mostly Cantonese as well) are around 400 presently.

There are some 3,000 ___E:Russians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russians)___ living in the city; as reported by the Russian Embassy in Havana, most are women married to Cubans who had studied in the Soviet Union.
Havana also shelters other non-Cuban population of an unknown size. There is a population of several thousand North African teen and pre-teen refugees.

Between 2018, the most recent census, and the mid-Twentieth Century census of 1953, Havana's population has grown by an estimated 87 percent, a growth rate typical of most ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ cities.
___E:Roman Catholics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic)___ form the largest religious group in Havana.
Havana is one of the three Metropolitan sees on the island (the others being Camagüey and Santiago), with two suffragan bishoprics: Matanzas and Pinar del Río.

Its patron saint is San Cristóbal ( ___E:Saint Christopher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Christopher)___ ), to whom the cathedral is devoted. it also has a ___E:minor basilica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_basilica)___ , ___E:Basílica Santuario Nacional de Nuestra Señora de la Caridad del Cobre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bas%C3%ADlica_Santuario_Nacional_de_Nuestra_Se%C3%B1ora_de_la_Caridad_del_Cobre)___ and two other national shrines, Jesús Nazareno del Rescate and San Lázaro (El Rincón).

It received papal visits from three successive supreme pontiffs: ___E:Pope John Paul II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II)___ (January 1998), ___E:Pope Benedict XVI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XVI)___ (March 2012) and ___E:Pope Francis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis)___ (September 2015).

The Jewish community in Havana has reduced after the Revolution from once having embraced more than 15,000 Jews, [citation needed] many of whom had fled ___E:Nazi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi)___ persecution and subsequently left Cuba to Miami or to Israel after Castro took to power in 1959. The city once had five synagogues, but only three remain (one ___E:Orthodox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Orthodox_Judaism)___ , and two ___E:Conservative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Judaism)___ : one Conservative ___E:Ashkenazi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi)___ and one Conservative ___E:Sephardic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardic)___ ), ___E:Beth Shalom Grand Synagogue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beth_Shalom_Temple_(Havana,_Cuba))___ is one of them and another that is a hybrid of all 3 put together.
In February 2007 the ___E:New York Times U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Times)___ estimated that there were about 1,500 known Jews living in Havana.

Havana has a diversified economy, with traditional sectors, such as manufacturing, construction, transportation and communications, and new or revived ones such as biotechnology and tourism. [citation needed]
The city's economy first developed on the basis of its location, which made it one of the early great trade centers in the New World.
Sugar and a flourishing ___E:slave U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave)___ trade first brought riches to the city, and later, after independence, it became a renowned resort.
Despite efforts by Fidel Castro's government to spread Cuba's industrial activity to all parts of the island, Havana remains the center of much of the nation's industry.
The traditional sugar industry, upon which the island's economy has been based for three centuries, is centered elsewhere on the island and controls some three-fourths of the export economy.
But light manufacturing facilities, meat-packing plants, and chemical and pharmaceutical operations are concentrated in Havana.

Other food-processing industries are also important, along with shipbuilding, vehicle manufacturing, production of alcoholic beverages (particularly rum), textiles, and tobacco products, particularly the world-famous ___E:Habanos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habanos_S.A.)___ cigars.

Although the ___E:harbors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harbor)___ of ___E:Cienfuegos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cienfuegos)___ and ___E:Matanzas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanzas)___ , in particular, have been developed under the revolutionary government, Havana remains Cuba's primary port facility; 50% of Cuban imports and exports pass through Havana.
The port also supports a considerable fishing industry. [citation needed]
In 2000, nearly 89% of the city's officially recorded labor force worked for government-run agencies, institutions or enterprises.
Havana, on average, has the country's highest incomes and human development indicators.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Cuba re-emphasized tourism as a major industry leading to its recovery.
Tourism is now Havana and Cuba's primary economic source.

Havana's economy is still in flux, despite Raúl Castro's embrace of free enterprise in 2011. Though there was an uptick in small businesses in 2011, many have since gone out of business, due to lack of business and income on the part of the local residents, whose salaries average $20 per month.
After the Revolution, Cuba's traditional capitalist free-enterprise system was replaced by a heavily socialized economic system.
In Havana, Cuban-owned businesses and U.S.-owned businesses were nationalized and today most businesses operate solely under state control. [citation needed]
In Old Havana and throughout Vedado there are several small private businesses, such as shoe-repair shops or dressmaking facilities.

Banking as well is also under state control, and the ___E:National Bank of Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bank_of_Cuba)___ , headquartered in Havana, is the control center of the Cuban economy.
Its branches in some cases occupy buildings that were in pre-revolutionary times the offices of Cuban or foreign banks. [citation needed]

In the late 1990s Vedado, located along the Atlantic waterfront, started to represent the principal commercial area. It was developed extensively between 1930 and 1960, when Havana developed as a major destination for U.S. tourists; high-rise hotels, ___E:casinos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino)___ , restaurants, and upscale commercial establishments, many reflecting the art deco style.

___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ is today Havana's financial district, and the main banks, airline companies offices, shops, most businesses headquarters, numerous high-rise apartments and hotels, are located in the area.  The University of Havana is located in Vedado.
The city has long been a popular attraction for tourists.
Between 1915 and 1930, Havana hosted more tourists than any other location in the ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ .

The influx was due in large part to ___E:Cuba's proximity to the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba-United_States_relations)___ , where restrictive ___E:prohibition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States)___ on ___E:alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug))___ and other pastimes stood in stark contrast to the island's traditionally relaxed attitude to leisure pursuits.
A pamphlet published by E.C.

Kropp Co., Milwaukee, WI, between 1921 and 1939 promoting tourism in Havana, Cuba, can be found in the University of Houston Digital Library, Havana, Cuba, The Summer Land of the World, Digital Collection.

With the deterioration of ___E:Cuba – United States relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba_%E2%80%93_United_States_relations)___ and the imposition of the ___E:trade embargo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_embargo_against_Cuba)___ on the island in 1961, tourism dropped drastically and did not return to anything close to its pre-revolution levels until 1989. The revolutionary government in general, and ___E:Fidel Castro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro)___ in particular, opposed any considerable development of tourism.
In 1982, the Cuban government passed a foreign investment code that opened a number of sectors to foreign capital. [citation needed]

Through the creation of firms open to such foreign investment (such as Cubanacan ), Cuba began to attract capital for hotel development, managing to increase the number of tourists from 130,000 (in 1980) to 326,000 (by the end of that decade).
Havana has also been a popular ___E:health tourism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_tourism)___ destination for more than 20 years.

Foreign patients travel to Cuba, Havana in particular, for a wide range of treatments including ___E:eye-surgery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye-surgery)___ , ___E:neurological U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurological)___ disorders such as ___E:multiple sclerosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_sclerosis)___ and ___E:Parkinson's disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_disease)___ , and ___E:orthopedics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthopaedics)___ .

Many patients are from Latin America, although medical treatment for ___E:retinitis pigmentosa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retinitis_pigmentosa)___ , often known as ___E:night blindness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_blindness)___ , has attracted many patients from Europe and North America.
Havana attracts over a million tourists annually,  the Official Census for Havana reports that in 2010 the city was visited by 1,176,627 international tourists,  a 20% increase from 2005.

The years after the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ collapsed in 1991, the city, and Cuba in general have suffered decades of economic deterioration, including ___E:Special Period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Period)___ of the 1990s.
The national government does not have an official definition of poverty.

The government researchers argue that "poverty" in most commonly accepted meanings does not really exist in Cuba, but rather that there is a sector of the population that can be described as "at risk" or "vulnerable" using internationally accepted measures.

The generic term " ___E:slum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slum)___ " is seldom used in Cuba, substandard housing is described: housing type, housing conditions, building materials, and settlement type. The National Housing Institute considers units in solares (a large inner-city mansion or older hotel or boarding house subdivided into rooms, sometimes with over 60 families)  and ___E:shanty towns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanty_towns)___ to be the "precarious housing stock" and tracks their number.

Most slum units are concentrated in the inner-city municipalities of ___E:Old Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Havana)___ and ___E:Centro Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centro_Habana)___ , as well as such neighborhoods as Atarés in ___E:Regla U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regla)___ .

People living in slums have access to the same education, health care, job opportunities and social security as those who live in formerly privileged neighborhoods. ___E:Shanty towns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanty_towns)___ are scattered throughout the city except for in a few central areas.
Over 9% of Havana's population live in cuartería ( solares, ciudadela ), 3.3% in ___E:shanty towns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanty_towns)___ , and 0.3% in refugee shelters.

This does not include an estimate of the number of people living in housing in "fair" or "poor" condition because in many cases these units do not necessarily constitute slum housing but rather are basically sound dwellings needing repairs.

According to Instituto Nacional de Vivienda (National Housing Institute) official figures, in 2001, 64% of Havana's 586,768 units were considered in "good" condition, up from 50% in 1990. Some 20% were in "fair" condition and 16% in "poor" condition.
Partial or total building collapses are not uncommon, although the number had been cut in half by the end of the 1990s as the worst units disappeared and others were repaired.
Buildings in Old Havana and Centro Habana are especially exposed to the elements: high humidity, the corrosive effects of salt spray from proximity to the coast, and occasional flooding.
Most areas of the city, especially the highly populated districts, are in ___E:urban decay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_decay)___ .
Havana is served by ___E:José Martí International Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mart%C3%AD_International_Airport)___ .

The Airport lies about 11 kilometers (7 mi) south of the city center, in the municipality of ___E:Boyeros U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyeros)___ , and is the main hub for the country's ___E:flag carrier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_carrier)___ ___E:Cubana de Aviación U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubana_de_Aviaci%C3%B3n)___ .

The airport is Cuba's main international and domestic gateway, it connects Havana with the rest of the ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ , ___E:North U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ , ___E:Central U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America)___ and South America, Europe and one destination in Africa.

The city is also served by ___E:Playa Baracoa Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playa_Baracoa_Airport)___ , a small airport to the west of city used for some domestic flights, primarily ___E:Aerogaviota U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerogaviota)___ .
Havana has a network of suburban, interurban and long-distance rail lines.
The railways are nationalized and run by the FFCC ( ___E:Ferrocarriles de Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrocarriles_de_Cuba)___ – Railways of Cuba).

The FFCC connects Havana with all the provinces of Cuba, and the ___E:Havana Suburban Railway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Suburban_Railway)___ serves the city. The main railway stations are: ___E:Central Rail Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Railway_Station,_Havana)___ , La Coubre Rail Station, ___E:Casablanca Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca,_Havana)___ , and Estación de Tulipán.

In 2004 the annual passenger volume was some 11 million,  but demand is estimated at two-and-a-half to three times this value, with the busiest route being between Havana and ___E:Santiago de Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_de_Cuba)___ , some 836 kilometers (519 mi) apart by rail. In 2000 the Union de Ferrocarriles de Cuba bought French first class airconditioned coaches.
New Chinese made and Russian made coaches for distance trains debuted in the 2010s, and some now serve suburban services.

In the 1980s there were plans for a ___E:Metro system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_Transit)___ in Havana similar to ___E:Moscow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Metro)___ 's, as a result of the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ influence in Cuba at the time. The studies of geology and finance made by Cuban, Czech and Soviet specialists were already well advanced in the 1980s.
The Cuban press showed the construction project and the course route, linking municipalities and neighborhoods in the capital.

In the late 1980s the project had already begun, each mile (1.6 km) of track was worth a million dollars at the time, but with the ___E:fall of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ in 1991 the project was later dropped.

An interurban line, [a] known as the ___E:Hershey Electric Railway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hershey_Electric_Railway)___ , built in 1917 runs from Casablanca (across the harbor from Old Havana) to Hershey and on to ___E:Matanzas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanzas)___ .

Havana operated a tram system until 1952, which began as a ___E:horsecar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsecar)___ system, Ferro Carril Urbano de la Habana in 1858,  merged with rival coach operator in 1863 as Empresa del Ferro-Carril Urbano y Omnibus de La Habana and later electrified in 1900 under new foreign owners as Havana Electric Railway Company.

Ridership decline resulted in bankruptcy in 1950 with new owner Autobus Modernos SA abandoning the systems in favor of buses and the remaining cars were sold to ___E:Matanzas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanzas)___ in 1952. [citation needed]

The city's road network is quite extensive, and has broad avenues, main streets and major access roads to the city such as the Autopista Nacional (A1), ___E:Carretera Central U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carretera_Central_(Cuba))___ and ___E:Via Blanca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Blanca_(Cuba))___ .
The road network has been under construction and growth since the Spanish era but is undergoing a major deterioration due to low maintenance.

The national government assumes all responsibility for education, and there are adequate primary, secondary, and vocational training schools throughout Cuba. The schools are of varying quality and education is free and compulsory at all levels except higher learning, which is also free.

The ___E:University of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Havana)___ , located in the ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ section of Havana, was established in 1728 and was regarded as a leading institution of higher learning in the ___E:Western Hemisphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Hemisphere)___ .
Soon after the Revolution, the university, as well as all other educational institutions, were nationalized.

Since then several other universities have opened, like the ___E:Higher Learning Polytechnic Institute José Antonio Echeverría U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytechnic_Jos%C3%A9_Antonio_Echeverr%C3%ADa)___ where the vast majority of today's Cuban engineers are taught.

The ___E:Cuban National Ballet School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_National_Ballet_School)___ with 4,350 students is one of the largest ballet schools in the world and the most prestigious ballet school in Cuba.

The coat of arms of Havana consists of three castles that represent the three castles that defended the city: the ___E:Fuerza Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillo_de_la_Real_Fuerza)___ , the ___E:Morro Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morro_Castle_(Havana))___ and the ___E:Punta Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador_de_la_Punta_Fortress)___ .
The key represents that Havana was the gateway to the ___E:New World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World)___ .

The shield, supported by an oak branch on one side and a ___E:laurel wreath U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_wreath)___ on the other, symbolizes the strength of the nation, the laurel wreath, honor, and glory.
These symbols represent the rights of man.
Havana has diverse styles of architecture, from castles built in the 16th century, to modernist high-rise buildings.

The present condition of many structures have deteriorated since 1959 or have been demolished, including the demolition of the ___E:Plaza del Vapor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Vapor,_Havana)___ , built in 1835 by the architect of the ___E:Palacio de la Marquesa de Villalba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Palacio_de_la_Marquesa_de_Villalba&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , Eugenio Rayneri Sorrentino, the father of ___E:Eugenio Rayneri Piedra U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Rayneri_Piedra)___ the architect of the ___E:El Capitolio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Capitolio)___ of 1929. The ___E:Plaza del Vapor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Vapor,_Havana)___ was demolished in 1959 by the new, revolutionary government. [b] [c] Numerous building collapses throughout the city have resulted in injuries and deaths due to a lack of maintenance.

Riches were brought from the Spanish into and through Havana as it was a key ___E:transshipment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transshipment)___ point between the ___E:New World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World)___ and ___E:Old World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World)___ .
As a result, Havana was the most heavily fortified city in the Americas.

Most examples of early architecture can be seen in military fortifications such as ___E:La Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Caba%C3%B1a)___ (1558–1577) designed by ___E:Battista Antonelli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battista_Antonelli)___ and the ___E:Castillo del Morro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morro_Castle_(Havana))___ (1589–1630).
This sits at the entrance of ___E:Havana Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Harbor)___ and provides an insight into the supremacy and wealth at that time.

Old Havana was also protected by a defensive wall begun in 1674 but had already overgrown its boundaries when it was completed in 1767, becoming the new neighborhood of ___E:Centro Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centro_Habana)___ .

The influence from different styles and cultures can be seen in Havana's Spanish architecture, with a diverse range of ___E:Mudéjar architecture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mud%C3%A9jar_art)___ , ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_architecture)___ , ___E:Italian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Italy)___ , ___E:Greek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_architecture)___ and ___E:Roman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_architecture)___ .

The ___E:San Carlos and San Ambrosio Seminary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Carlos_and_San_Ambrosio_Seminary)___ (18th century) is a good example of early Spanish influenced architecture. ___E:The Havana cathedral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_Havana)___ (1748–1777) dominating the Plaza de la Catedral (1749) is the best example of Cuban Baroque.
Surrounding it are the former palaces of the Count de Casa-Bayona (1720–1746) Marquis de Arcos (1746) and the Marquis de Aguas Claras (1751–1775).

The ___E:Iglesia del Espíritu Santo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iglesia_del_Esp%C3%ADritu_Santo,_Havana)___ was devoted in 1638. The Espíritu Santo contains some notable paintings including a seated, post-crucifixion Christ on the right wall, and catacombs.

It is considered one of the oldest temples in Havana and it is said that its main interest lies essentially in the simplicity of the beautiful stone construction. [citation needed] The church was rebuilt and expanded in 1648 and given the rank of a parish.

During the Spanish era it had exceptional importance, since by a ___E:Papal Bull U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_Bull)___ of 1772 and a Royal Certificate of 1773, of ___E:Charles III of Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain)___ , it was declared "Única Iglesia inmune en esta ciudad, construida en 1855." ("the only immune church in this city, built-in 1855."), which meant that any persecuted individual could find Amparo (sanctuary) in it against the action of the authorities or of justice.

A metal plaque at the foot of the bell tower attests to this fact. [citation needed] The Iglesia del Espíritu Santo's greatest interest from an architectural point of view lies in the simplicity of the coral stone construction and the lack of lavish decoration.  [d] Other elements of great importance are the funerary crypts that were discovered in 1953. The crypt is from times before the ___E:Colón Cemetery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colon_Cemetery,_Havana)___ (1876) in El Vedado was built.

The ___E:Alameda de Paula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Alameda_de_Paula,_Havana)___ was the first promenade in Cuba, designed and constructed in 1776 by Antonio Fernández Trevejo, following the instructions of the ___E:Laureano de Torres y Ayala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureano_de_Torres_y_Ayala)___ , it was created on the site of the old Rincón refuse dump. It was an embankment with two rows of poplar trees and some benches, it became one of Havana's most important social and cultural spaces, it was the model of the ___E:Paseo del Prado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paseo_del_Prado,_Havana)___ designed in 1925. It was given the name Alameda de Paula because of its proximity to the old Hospital and Iglesia of San Francisco de Paula.

Between 1803 and 1805 the pavement was tiled, a fountain and stone benches, lampposts and the marble column were added, it qualified as a pleasant entertainment for the residents of the ___E:Villa de San Cristóbal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Havana)___ , lacking recreational sites at that time. In 1841, the stairs that gave access to the promenade were widened and several lampposts were added.
In the year 2000, the Havana promenade was restored and extended until it reached the Iglesia de San Francisco de Paula.

Towards the end of the 17th century, the first stone of what would be the hospital for women and the ___E:church of San Francisco de Paula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iglesia_de_San_Francisco_de_Paula,_Havana)___ was placed, the buildings were expanded in 1731 with the support and donations from the City Council and orders of the different General Captains in command of the island.

In 1776, it was the most important hospital in Havana, there were several generations of famous doctors that trained here.  The ___E:Presbyter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyter)___ of the ___E:Cathedral of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Cathedral)___ , don Nicolás Estévez Borges, in 1664 ordered the construction of a Hospital for Women and an adjoining church devoted to ___E:Saint Francis of Paola U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Paola)___ who was one of the founders of the Roman Catholic Order of the ___E:Minims U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minim_(religious_order))___ . [e] Both buildings were completely destroyed by a hurricane in 1730 and were rebuilt and enlarged in 1745 in the Baroque style seen today.

___E:Neoclassism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture)___ was introduced into the city in the 1840s, at the time including Gas public lighting in 1848 and the railroad in 1837. In the second half of the 18th century, sugar and coffee production increased rapidly, which became essential in the development of Havana's most prominent architectural style.

Many wealthy Habaneros took their inspiration from the French; this can be seen within the interiors of upper-class houses such as the Aldama Palace built in 1844. This is considered the most important neoclassical residential building in Cuba and typifies the design of many houses of this period with portales of neoclassical columns facing open spaces or courtyards.

In 1925 ___E:Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Nicolas_Forestier)___ , the head of urban planning in Paris moved to Havana for five years to collaborate with architects and landscape designers.
In the master planning of the city his aim was to create a harmonic balance between the classical built form and the tropical landscape.
He embraced and connected the city's road networks while accentuating prominent landmarks.
His influence has left a huge mark on Havana although many of his ideas were cut short by the ___E:Great Depression in 1929 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ .
During the first decades of the 20th century Havana expanded more rapidly than at any time during its history.
Great wealth prompted architectural styles to be influenced from abroad.
The peak of Neoclassicism came with the construction of the ___E:Vedado district U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ (begun in 1859).
This area features a number of set back well-proportioned buildings in the Neoclassical style.

Built in 1875, in the Reparto de las Las Murallas, (wide strip of land that remained after the city walls were demolished in 1863), it was the work of the architect Eugenio Rayneri y Sorrentino. [f] Around 1880 the mansion was owned by the Count of Casa Moré.
The "La Flor de José Murias" tobacco factory was installed in the building.
Later, through the exploitation of rents, it became a tenement house.
In 1951 some of its spaces were dedicated to housing.
On its upper floor, the Spanish Center and the Israeli Center of Cuba had their headquarters.

The palace of the Marquesa de Villalba and the ___E:Mercado de Tacón U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Vapor,_Havana)___ were designed by the Eugenio Rayneri y Sorrentino at almost the same time, 1875 and 1876, respectively, each in a style that accommodated the particular typology (residential and commercial) thus conceiving each work with the formal element accommodating different aesthetic requirements.
The property is, after the ___E:Aldama Palace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palacio_de_Aldama)___ , the strongest example of Cuban Neoclassicism.
The palace of the Marquesa de Villalba is in the neoclassical style, perhaps only comparable in Havana – according to Alina Castellanos – to the Aldama Palace.

But while the latter limits the decoration to the natural slenderness of the colonnade, in the most classical way of the Greek Parthenon, the former uses Roman and Renaissance elaborations, hence, the arcade has been projected on pillars, the building was crowned with a considerable cornice.

The neoclassical decoration can also be seen in the window covers, which take alternate forms of a triangular or semicircular pediment, and glass over the door, similar to the ___E:Plaza del Vapor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Vapor,_Havana)___ .

The ___E:Palacio de Aldama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palacio_de_Aldama)___ is a neoclassical mansion located diagonally opposite to the old ___E:Plaza del Vapor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_del_Vapor,_Havana)___ (Parque del Curita), and in front of the old ___E:Campo de Marte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campo_de_Marte,_Havana)___ ; present day Parque de la Fraternidad, in Havana, Cuba. Built in 1840 by the Dominican architect and engineer Manuel José Carrera, its main facade of columns spans one block on Calle Amistad between Calles Reina and Estrella.
The Royal Palm Hotel is located on the corner of San Rafael and Industria.
It was inaugurated as "Edificio Luis. E. del Valle", in honor of the sugar magnate who owned the building.
It was soon sold to Canadian Wilbur E. Todgham, however, who turned it into the famed Royal Palm Hotel.
The commercial function of the ground floor has been preserved to date, taking advantage of its excellent location on Boulevard de San Rafael.

Taking into account the architectural values of this building and its socio-cultural importance within the urban landscape in which it is located, the building received a major restoration in 2000, with the support of the Provincial Council of Seville, Spain.

The ___E:Bacardi Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacardi_Building_(Havana))___ ( Edificio Bacardí ) is Havana landmark designed by the architects Esteban Rodríguez-Castells and Rafael Fernández Ruenes and completed in 1930.  It is located on the corner of Calles Monserrate and San Juan de Dios on a 1,320 sq meter lot in Las Murallas, ___E:Old Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Havana)___ .
The building is in the ___E:art deco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_deco)___ style that was popular internationally in the early decades of the 20th century.

The Bacardi Building was designed to be the headquarters for the ___E:Bacardi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacardi)___ Rum Company; it was nationalized by the Castro government in the early 1960s.
In 2001, the building was restored by an Italian construction firm. The interior retains the original decorations in marble and granite.
It is regarded as one of the finest ___E:Art Deco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco)___ buildings in Latin America.

Designed by the architect Ricardo Mira in 1929, who in 1941 designed La Moderna Poesia bookstore on Obispo Street for the same owner, the ___E:López Serrano Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B3pez_Serrano_Building)___ was the tallest residential building in Cuba until the construction of the ___E:FOCSA Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FOCSA_Building)___ in 1956. The construction of the building was promoted by José Antonio López Serrano, a publisher who ran La Moderna Poesía.

Known by buildings of high-quality, ___E:modernist architecture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture)___ transformed much of the city. Examples are the Havana ___E:Hilton Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilton_Hotel)___ of (1958), the ___E:Radiocentro CMQ Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocentro_CMQ_Building)___ of 1955 by ___E:Martín Domínguez Esteban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mart%C3%ADn_Dom%C3%ADnguez_Esteban)___ architect of the ___E:FOCSA Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FOCSA_Building)___ in 1956, and the ___E:Edificio del Seguro Médico, Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edificio_del_Seguro_M%C3%A9dico,_Havana)___ by ___E:Antonio Quintana Simonetti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Quintana_Simonetti)___ . Hotel ___E:Tryp Habana Libre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tryp_Habana_Libre)___ is one of the larger hotels in ___E:Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba)___ , situated in ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ , Havana.

The hotel has 572 rooms  in a 25-floor tower at Calle 23 ("La Rampa") and Calle L. Opened in 1958 as the Habana Hilton, the hotel famously served as the residence of ___E:Fidel Castro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro)___ and other revolutionaries throughout 1959, after their capture of Havana.
The Habana Hilton was constructed at a cost of $24 million, under the personal auspices of President ___E:Fulgencio Batista U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulgencio_Batista)___ .

It was built as an investment by the Caja de Retiro y Asistencia Social de los Trabajadores Gastronomicos,  the pension plan of the Cuban catering workers' union, with additional financing from the Banco de Fomento Agricola e Industrial de Cuba (BANFAIC).

It was operated by the American ___E:Hilton Hotels International U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilton_Hotels_%26_Resorts)___ group and was designed by the well-known Los Angeles architect ___E:Welton Becket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welton_Becket)___ , who had previously designed the ___E:Beverly Hilton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hilton)___ for the chain.
Becket designed the 27-story Habana Hilton in collaboration with Havana-based architects Lin Arroyo,  and Gabriela Menéndez.
Arroyo was the Minister of Public Works under Batista.
The hotel was constructed by the ___E:Frederick Snare Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Snare_Corporation)___ .

The ___E:Radiocentro CMQ Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocentro_CMQ_Building)___ complex is a former radio and television production facility and office building at the intersection of Calle L and ___E:La Rampa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rampa)___ in ___E:El Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Vedado)___ , Cuba. It was modeled after ___E:Raymond Hood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Hood)___ 's 1933 ___E:Rockefeller Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center)___ in New York City.  With 1,650 seats, the theater first opened on 23 December 1947, under the name Teatro Warner Radiocentro, it was owned by brothers Goar and ___E:Abel Mestre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Abel_Mestre&action=edit&redlink=1)___ .
Today the building serves as the headquarters of the ___E:Cuban Institute of Radio and Television U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Institute_of_Radio_and_Television)___ (ICRT).

For the construction of this building, the Havana building authorities granted a permit in 1947 amending the ordinances that were then in effect in ___E:El Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Vedado)___ prohibiting the construction of buildings of more than three storeys.
This statute was modified six years later to expand the construction of up to four floors because many planners and owners claimed the need to authorize them to build taller buildings in the area.

The ___E:FOCSA Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FOCSA_Building)___ is a residential block in the Vedado neighborhood of Havana, Cuba. It was named after the contracting company Fomento de Obras y Construcciones, Sociedad Anónima , and the architects were Ernesto Gómez Sampera (1921–2004), Mercedes Diaz (his wife), and ___E:Martín Domínguez Esteban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mart%C3%ADn_Dom%C3%ADnguez_Esteban)___ (1897–1970), who was the architect of the ___E:Radiocentro CMQ Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocentro_CMQ_Building)___ .

The structural engineer was Luis Sáenz Duplace, of the firm Sáenz, Cancio & Martín, and professor of engineering at the ___E:University of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Havana)___ .
The civil engineers were Bartolome Bestard and Manuel Padron.
Gustavo Becquer and Fernando H. Meneses were the mechanical and electrical engineers, respectively.
It is located on a site bordered by Calles 17 and M and Calles 19 and N in the ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ .

The ___E:Edificio Focsa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FOCSA_Building)___ (1956) represents Havana's economic dominance at the time. This 35-story complex was conceived and based on Corbusian ideas of a self-contained city within a city. It contained 400 apartments, garages, a school, a supermarket, and a restaurant on the top floor.
This was the tallest high-strength concrete structure in the world at the time (using no steel frame).

The ___E:Edificio del Seguro Médico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edificio_del_Seguro_M%C3%A9dico)___ is a commercial building in El ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ , Havana.

Built between 1955 and 1958, it was designed as a mixed use building for apartments and offices for the headquarters of the National Medical Insurance Company by ___E:Antonio Quintana Simonetti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Quintana_Simonetti)___ .

Contemporary Havana can essentially be described as three cities in one: ___E:Old Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Havana)___ , ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ , and the newer suburban districts.
Old Havana, with its narrow streets and overhanging balconies, is the traditional center of part of Havana's commerce, industry, and entertainment, as well as being a residential area.
To the west a newer section, centered on the uptown area known as ___E:Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedado)___ , has become the rival of Old Havana for commercial activity and nightlife.

The ___E:Capitolio Nacional U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Capitol_Building_(Havana))___ building marks the beginning of Centro Habana, a working-class neighborhood that lies between Vedado and Old Havana.
Barrio Chino and the ___E:Real Fabrica de Tabacos Partagás U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Fabrica_de_Tabacos_Partag%C3%A1s)___ , one of Cuba's oldest cigar factories is located in the area.

A third Havana is that of the more affluent residential and industrial districts that spread out mostly to the west. Among these is ___E:Marianao U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marianao)___ , one of the newer parts of the city, dating mainly from the 1920s.
Some of the suburban exclusivity was lost after the revolution, many of the suburban homes having been nationalized by the Cuban government to serve as schools, hospitals, and government offices.

Several private country clubs were converted to public recreational centers. ___E:Miramar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miramar,_Havana)___ , located west of Vedado along the coast, remains Havana's exclusive area; mansions, foreign embassies, diplomatic residences, upscale shops, and facilities for wealthy foreigners are common in the area.  The ___E:International School of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_School_of_Havana)___ is located in the Miramar neighborhood.

In the 1980s many parts of ___E:Old Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Havana)___ , including the Plaza de Armas, became part of a projected 35-year multimillion-dollar restoration project, for Cubans to appreciate their past and boost tourism.
In the past ten years [which?] , with the assistance of foreign aid and under the support of local city historian Eusebio Leal Spengler, large parts of Habana Vieja have been renovated.

The city is moving forward with their renovations, with most of the major plazas (Plaza Vieja, Plaza de la Catedral, Plaza de San Francisco and Plaza de Armas) and major tourist streets (Obispo and Mercaderes) near completion.

The ___E:Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes de La Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_Nacional_de_Bellas_Artes_de_La_Habana)___ is a Fine Arts museum that exhibits Cuban and international art. The museum houses one of the largest collections of paintings and sculpture from Latin America and is the largest in the Caribbean region.

Under the Cuban Ministry of Culture , it occupies two locations in the vicinity of Havana's Paseo del Prado , these are the Palace of Fine Arts , devoted to Cuban art and the Palace of the Asturian Center , dedicated to universal art.  Its artistic heritage is made up of over 45,000 pieces.

Since 1995 the capital hosts the headquarters of the ___E:Ludwig Foundation of Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ludwig_Foundation_of_Cuba)___ in Vedado, founded by the German collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig, it is a non-governmental and non-profit organization for the dissemination and protection of Cuban art. Notable artists associated with the city include ___E:Federico Beltrán Masses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Beltr%C3%A1n_Masses)___ ,   ___E:Víctor Manuel García Valdés U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctor_Manuel_Garc%C3%ADa_Vald%C3%A9s)___ ,   and ___E:Wifredo Lam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wifredo_Lam)___ .

Facing Havana's Central Park is the ___E:baroque U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture)___ ___E:Gran Teatro de La Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Teatro_de_La_Habana)___ , a prominent theater built in 1837.  It is now home of the ___E:National Ballet of Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_National_Ballet)___ and the ___E:International Ballet Festival of Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Ballet_Festival_of_Havana)___ , one of the oldest in the New World.
The façade of the building is adorned with a stone and marble statue.
There are also sculptural pieces by ___E:Giuseppe Moretti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Moretti)___ ,  representing allegories depicting benevolence, education, music and theater.
The principal theater is the ___E:García Lorca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Garc%C3%ADa_Lorca)___ Auditorium, with seats for 1,500 and balconies.

Glories of its rich history; the Italian ___E:tenor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor)___ ___E:Enrico Caruso U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Caruso)___ sang, the Russian ballerina ___E:Anna Pavlova U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Pavlova)___ danced, and the French ___E:Sarah Bernhardt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt)___ acted.

___E:Alicia Alonso U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Alonso)___ was a Cuban prima ballerina assoluta and choreographer whose company became the ___E:Ballet Nacional de Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_National_Ballet)___ in 1955.  Alonso was born "on the outskirts" of Havana in 1920  She is best known for her portrayals of ___E:Giselle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giselle)___ and ___E:the ballet version of Carmen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Suite_(ballet))___ .

CMQ was a Cuban radio and television station located in Havana, ___E:Cuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba)___ , reaching an audience in the 1940s and 1950s, attracting viewers and listeners with a program that ranged from music and news dissemination.
It later expanded into radio and television networks.
As a radio network it was a heated competitor of the ___E:RHC-Cadena Azul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RHC-Cadena_Azul)___ network.
The company was founded on March 12, 1933, by Miguel Gabriel and Ángel Cambó.
Ten years later, on August 1, 1943, half of it was acquired by the business group of ___E:Goar Mestre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goar_Mestre)___ .
In the beginning, it transmitted only in the capital expanding later to the rest of the country.
Pre-revolutionary Cuba was an early adopter of new technology, including TV. Cuba was the first Latin American country to have television.
In December 1946 station CM-21P conducted an experimental multi-point live broadcast.
Regular commercial broadcasting began in October 1950 with Gaspar Pumarejo's ___E:Unión Radio TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Uni%C3%B3n_Radio_TV&action=edit&redlink=1)___ .

This was followed by Goar Mestre Espinosa's CMQ-TV on channel 6 on 18 December 1950. CMQ officially launched on 11 March 1951, and would become an ___E:NBC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC)___ affiliate.
By 1954, CMQ-TV had expanded into a seven station network.
With the CMQ network, Cuba the second country in the world, only after the United States, to have a national TV network.

At the beginning of the 1950s with the transmission of the novel El Derecho de Nacer , by Felix B. Caignet, displaced the competing station, RHC Cadena Azul. It is with this leadership that the second Cuban television channel, CMQ TV, Channel 6 is born. It was initially located on Calle Monte, on the corner of Paseo del Prado.

On 12 March 1948, the radio studio was moved to the ___E:Radiocentro building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocentro_CMQ_Building)___ in La Rampa and Calle L in ___E:El Vedado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Vedado)___ . [citation needed]
The Havana Film Festival is a Cuban festival that focuses on the promotion of Latin American filmmakers.
It is also known in Spanish as Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano de La Habana, and in English as International Festival of New Latin American Cinema of Havana.
It takes place every year during December in the city of ___E:Havana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Havana)___ , Cuba.

The inaugural International Festival of New Latin American Cinema was held on 3 December 1979, and more than 600 film directors of Latin America responded to the first call made by the ___E:Cuban Institute of the Cinematographic Art and Industry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Institute_of_the_Cinematographic_Art_and_Industry)___ (ICAIC).

Its founders the included President of ICAIC, Alfredo Guevara, and the filmmakers ___E:Julio García Espinosa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Garc%C3%ADa_Espinosa)___ and ___E:Pastor Vega U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastor_Vega)___ .

As expressed in its founding convocation, the festival aimed to "promote the regular meeting of Latin American filmmakers who with their work enrich the artistic culture of our countries (…); ensure the joint presentation of fiction films, documentaries, cartoons and current events (…), and contribute to the international diffusion and circulation of the main and most significant productions of our cinematographies".
In 2013 the Havana Film Festival announced that it was reappointing Iván Giroud as its president.
Giroud had previously served as president from 1994 to 2010.

All Cuban residents have free access to health care in hospitals,  local polyclinics, and neighborhood family doctors who serve on average 170 families each,  which is one of the highest doctor-to-patient ratio in the world.

Nonetheless, the health system has suffered from shortages of supplies, equipment and medications caused by ending of the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ subsidies in the early 1990s and the ___E:US embargo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_embargo_against_Cuba)___ .

Nevertheless, Havana's ___E:infant mortality rate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infant_mortality_rate)___ in 2009 was 4.9 per 1,000 live births,  5.12 in the country as a whole, which is lower than many ___E:developed nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country)___ ,   and the lowest in the ___E:developing world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country)___ .
Administration of the health care system for the nation is centered largely in Havana.
Hospitals in Havana are run by the national government, and citizens are assigned hospitals and clinics to which they may go for attention. [citation needed]
Many Cubans are avid sports fans who particularly favor baseball.

Havana's team in the ___E:Cuban National Series U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_National_Series)___ is ___E:Industriales U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industriales)___ , one of the most successful teams in the tournament.

In the past, it has also been represented by ___E:Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habana_(Cuban_League))___ (in the pre-revolutionary ___E:Cuban League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_League)___ ) as well as ___E:Metropolitanos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitanos)___ and ___E:La Habana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Habana_(Cuban_National_Series))___ in the National Series.

The city has several large sports stadiums, the largest one being the ___E:Estadio Latinoamericano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Latinoamericano)___ , where Industriales play. Admission to sporting events is generally free, and impromptu games are played in neighborhoods throughout the city. Social clubs at the beaches provide facilities for water sports and include restaurants and dance halls.
